sweep_summary: Ono (onoo1246) is in the catalog as fixed-strict (initial primary, alternating secondary) on Phinnemore 1985:174. this search of works with stress in the title's two title hits are both artefacts of Glottolog's computerized tagging: ref 9757 is a SIL-PNG bibliography line that glued Phinnemore 1985 onto Pike & Scott 1963's Fore pitch accent paper (the 'accent' keyword, vol.16 and pp.179-89 belong to the Fore paper), and ref 673622 (Kemler Nelson et al. 1989, English motherese; Crossref abstract read) is tagged Ono from the title word 'might'.; also ANU handle 1885/254465), was copied into our files, and its stress section (pp.174-175) was read on 110-dpi page renders: primary stress regularly on the first syllable of the word, secondary on alternating syllables (3rd; 3rd/5th/both in 5+-syllable words), 'Stress is predictable' -- confirming the catalog's classification verbatim; a partial Rosetta Project scan (pp.181-187, no stress passage) was also downloaded from archive.org. Nothing new to acquire from this search of works with stress in the title; the earlier works still to obtain (Phinnemore 1976 UND thesis, restricted to Harvard/ProQuest; Wacke 1930-31 ZfES 21, not online) remain low priority. UND commons, HathiTrust catalog and sil.org returned not reachable by automated download. txt, p-02/p-03 renders, rosettaproject_ons_phon-1.*).

new_statements.quote: Primary stress occurs regularly on the first syllable of stress group while secondary stress falls on subsequent alternating syllables. Juncture (indicated by space) is the boundary of the stress group. [...] Stress is predictable. [...] Three and four syllable words carry primary stress on the initial syllable and secondary stress on the third syllable. [p.175] In words of five or more syllables primary stress remains on the first syllable with secondary stress occuring on either the third or fifth syllable or both.
new_statements.citation: Phinnemore, Thomas R. 1985. Ono phonology and morphophonemics. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 22 (Pacific Linguistics A-63): 173-214.
new_statements.reading: Fixed initial primary stress on the word (the author's 'stress group', glossed 'word'), quantity-insensitive and fully predictable, with secondary stress on alternating odd syllables from the third; in five-or-more-syllable words the secondary stress may sit on the 3rd, the 5th, or both. This supports the catalog's fixed-strict, initial-primary coding (rule 10/101/1010/10101..). The one nuance is the domain: pause-less N+N sequences fuse into a single stress group with one initial stress (ŋéiŋerèp 'people'), and a phrase-initial monosyllable takes the stress while the next word is 'lenis'; this is a phrase-level fusion, not lexical or variable word stress. Verified first-hand on the page images this search of works with stress in the title.

audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-strict, initial primary + alternating secondary, rule 10/101/1010/10101..) rests, through StressTyp2, on Phinnemore 1985:174-175, a dedicated 42-pp phonology article that is the best description Glottolog knows for Ono; we hold it (, CC BY-SA sealang copy) and the stress passage is confirmed verbatim at the stated pages. Primary stress is categorically initial ('Stress is predictable'; 'Primary stress occurs regularly on the first syllable'), so the fixed: initial syllable coding is safe; the only nuance — secondary stress in 5+-syllable words on the 3rd, 5th, or both — is already recorded in the corr note, so no reclassification is warranted. The record's weakness is clerical, not evidential: quote/cite/loc/grade are empty and 'ver' points to the database. sources.note: Word-level ('stress group (word)') primary stress is categorically on the first syllable; secondary stress on alternating syllables (3rd in 3-4-syllable words; 3rd, 5th or both in 5+-syllable words); stress is predictable, no quantity condition stated (syllable template (C)V(V)(C), complex nuclei 'the same length as the simple nucleus').
